```{r}
  "knitr", "tidyverse", "vegan", "permute",
  "ggrepel", "grid", "dplyr", "readxl", "glmmTMB",
  "DHARMa", "car", "emmeans"

# Already installed?

  packages_required, 
  FUN = requireNamespace, 
  FUN.VALUE = TRUE, 
  quietly = TRUE
) 
# Install missing packages
install.packages(names(packages_installed)[!packages_installed])

# Chunk font size hook: allows size='small'

knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  chunk = function(x, options) {
    x <- def.chunk.hook(x, options)
    ifelse(
      options$size == "normalsize", 
      yes = x,
      no = paste0("\n \\", options$size, "\n\n", x, "\n\n \\normalsize")
    )
  }
)

#load all packages

# Set output width to prevent long model summaries overflowing PDF margins
knitr::opts_chunk$set(width = 65)

#set seed for reproducible simulations throughout the document
set.seed(123)
```

```{r}
#| label: Load and set variable types
df <- read_excel("../data/macrofaune_counts.xlsx")
df[7:ncol(df)] <- lapply(df[7:ncol(df)], as.numeric)
df[c(1, 3:6)] <- lapply(df[c(1, 3:6)], as.factor)
str(df)
```

# Statistical Analysis

## Explorative Analysis

### Key values

### PCA

## GLMM with abundances

### Data preparation for GLMM:

```{r}
#| label: Preparing data for GLMM
# identify taxa columns
taxa_cols <- names(df)[7:34]

# long-format dataset
df_long <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(taxa_cols),
    names_to = "taxon",
    values_to = "count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    taxon = factor(taxon)
  )

# sample-level abundance (per m²)
df_total <- df %>%
  mutate(
    total_count = rowSums(
      across(all_of(taxa_cols)),
      na.rm = FALSE
    ),
    density = total_count * 16, #25x25cm monoliths = 1/16 m²
    soil_type = factor(soil_type),
    layer = factor(layer, levels = c("L", "10", "20")),
    monolith_ID = factor(monolith_ID)
  )
```

### GLMM global

#### Fitting the models:

Models to investigate effects of soil_type and layer on abundance.
Poisson and negative binomial models are considered since abundances are counts and there may be a tendency to overdispersion or zero-inflation.

```{r}
#| label: Fitting total abundance models
# M1: Poisson, additive effects
m_p_add <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M2: Poisson, interaction
m_p_int <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
m_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
m_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)
```

#### Comparing models using Akaike's An Information Criterion

```{r}
#| label: Global model comparison using AIC
AIC_values <- AIC(m_p_add, m_p_int, m_nb_add, m_nb_int)

AIC_values$delta_AIC <- AIC_values$AIC - min(AIC_values$AIC)

AIC_values[order(AIC_values$AIC), ]
```

Negative binomial distribution is strongly preferred according to AIC and is retained.

#### Comparing nb additive vs. model with interaction:

```{r}
#| label: LRT for global abundance models

anova(m_nb_add, m_nb_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT
```

Given the interactive model has a higher AIC and does not significantly improve model fit compared to additive model (according to LRT), m_nb_add is retained.

#### Model diagnostics with DHARMa:

```{r}
#| label: Total abundance model diagnostics (including overdispersion + zero-inflation) with DHARMa

res_nb <- simulateResiduals(m_nb_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_nb)

testDispersion(res_nb)
testZeroInflation(res_nb)
```

No significant deviations detected, model is retained.

#### Investigation of model estimates:

```{r}
#| label: Total abundance model effects
Anova(m_nb_add)
summary(m_nb_add)
```

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a highly significant effect of soil layer on total soil macrofauna abundance (χ² = 106.85, df = 2, p \< 0.001).
The effect of soil type was not significant (χ² = 0.52, df = 1, p = 0.469).
Estimated random-effect variance (monolith) was 0.437 (SD = 0.661), indicating variation in baseline macrofauna abundance among monoliths.

#### Pairwise testing for layers:

```{r}
#| label: Pairwise testing using emmeans for total abundance
# Estimated marginal means for layers (response scale)
emm_layers <- emmeans(m_nb_add, ~ layer, type = "response")

# Pairwise comparisons (Tukey correction)
pairwise_layers <- as.data.frame(
  pairs(emmeans(m_nb_add, ~ layer), adjust = "tukey")
)

# Back-transform estimates to abundance ratios
pairwise_layers$ratio <- exp(pairwise_layers$estimate)
pairwise_layers

# Plot estimated abundance on the response scale
plot(emm_layers)
```

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment shows that macrofauna abundance was significantly higher in layer 10 than in layers L (7.42 times) and 20 (6.18 times), while no significant difference was found between layers L and 20 (p = 0.714).

### GLMM ecosystem engineers

#### Formicidae (Ants)

```{r}
#| label: Select ant data, run models and compare with AIC

df_ants <- df_total %>%
  select(Formicidae, layer, monolith_ID, soil_type)

# M1: Poisson, additive effects
ants_p_add <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M2: Poisson, interaction
ants_p_int <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
ants_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
ants_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

AIC_ants <- AIC(ants_p_add, ants_p_int, ants_nb_add,ants_nb_int)

AIC_ants$delta_AIC <- AIC_ants$AIC - min(AIC_ants$AIC)

AIC_ants[order(AIC_ants$AIC), ]
```

We keep the negative binomial distribution for the engineers because the AIC is lower that Poisson distribution models.

```{r}
#| label: LRT and DHARMa residual diagnostics for ant models

anova(ants_nb_add, ants_nb_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT

res_nb_ants <- simulateResiduals(ants_nb_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_nb_ants)

testDispersion(res_nb_ants)
testZeroInflation(res_nb_ants)

```

Quantile deviation detected (upper quantile specifically).
Some relatively high-abundance observations may not be adequately captured by the model.
Since all the other tests do not show any significant issues, ants_nb_add is retained as best-supported model regardless, though unexplained structure might remain.

```{r}
#| label: Model effects and pairwise comparison for ant model

Anova(ants_nb_add)
summary(ants_nb_add)

# Estimated marginal means for layers (response scale)
emm_layers_ants <- emmeans(ants_nb_add, ~ layer, type = "response")

# Pairwise comparisons (Tukey correction)
pairwise_layers_ants <- as.data.frame(
  pairs(emmeans(ants_nb_add, ~ layer), adjust = "tukey")
)

# Back-transform estimates to abundance ratios
pairwise_layers_ants$ratio <- exp(pairwise_layers_ants$estimate)
pairwise_layers_ants

# Plot estimated abundance on the response scale
plot(emm_layers_ants)
```

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a highly significant effect of soil layer on ant abundance (χ² = 28.00, df = 2, p \< 0.001).
The effect of soil type was not significant (χ² = 0.48, df = 1, p = 0.486).
The estimated random-effect variance for monolith was 0.655 (SD = 0.810), indicating variation in baseline ant abundance among monoliths.

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment showed that ant abundance was significantly higher in layer 10 than in layer L (5.05 times) and layer 20 (3.27 times), while no significant difference was found between layers L and 20 (p = 0.3995).

#### Isoptera (Termites)

```{r}

# M2: Poisson, interaction
termites_p_int <- glmmTMB(

  data = df_termites
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
termites_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  Isoptera ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_termites
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
termites_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  Isoptera~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_termites
)

AIC_termites <- AIC(termites_p_add, termites_p_int,
                    termites_nb_add,termites_nb_int)

AIC_termites$delta_AIC <- AIC_termites$AIC - min(AIC_termites$AIC)

AIC_termites[order(AIC_termites$AIC), ]
```

We keep the negative binomial distribution for the engineers because the AIC is lower that Poisson distribution models.

```{r}
#| label: LRT and DHARMa residual diagnostics for termite models

anova(termites_nb_add, termites_nb_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT

res_nb_termites <- simulateResiduals(termites_nb_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_nb_termites)

testDispersion(res_nb_termites)
testZeroInflation(res_nb_termites)
```

termites_nb_add is retained since adding the interaction does not significantly improve model fit and DHARMa model diagnostics are valid.

```{r}
#| label: Model effects and pairwise comparison for termite model 
Anova(termites_nb_add)
summary(termites_nb_add)

# Estimated marginal means for layers (response scale)
emm_layers_termites <- emmeans(termites_nb_add, ~ layer, type = "response")

# Pairwise comparisons (Tukey correction)
pairwise_layers_termites <- as.data.frame(
  pairs(emmeans(termites_nb_add, ~ layer), adjust = "tukey")
)

# Back-transform estimates to abundance ratios
pairwise_layers_termites$ratio <- exp(pairwise_layers_termites$estimate)
pairwise_layers_termites

# Plot estimated abundance on the response scale
plot(emm_layers_termites)
```

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a highly significant effect of soil layer on termite abundance (χ² = 36.56, df = 2, p \< 0.001).
The effect of soil type was not significant (χ² = 0.89, df = 1, p = 0.347).
The estimated random-effect variance for monolith was effectively zero (8.22 × 10⁻⁹; SD = 0.00009), indicating virtually no remaining variation in baseline termite abundance among monoliths after accounting for the fixed effects.

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment showed that termite abundance was significantly higher in layer 10 than in layer L (18.08 times) and layer 20 (745.48 times; estimated richness for 20 nearing zero).
Abundance was also significantly higher in layer L than in layer 20 (41.23 times; all p ≤ 0.0073).

#### Lumbricina oligochaetes (Earthworms)

```{r}
#| label: Earthworm data, fit models, test (AIC + LRT)
df_earthworms <- df_total %>%
  select(Lumbricina_oligochaetes, layer, monolith_ID, soil_type)


# M1: Poisson, additive effects
earthworms_p_add <- glmmTMB(
  Lumbricina_oligochaetes ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_earthworms
)

# M2: Poisson, interaction
earthworms_p_int <- glmmTMB(
  Lumbricina_oligochaetes ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_earthworms
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
earthworms_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  Lumbricina_oligochaetes ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_earthworms
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
earthworms_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  Lumbricina_oligochaetes~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_earthworms
)

AIC_earthworms <- AIC(earthworms_p_add, earthworms_p_int,
                      earthworms_nb_add,earthworms_nb_int)

AIC_earthworms$delta_AIC <- AIC_earthworms$AIC - min(AIC_earthworms$AIC)

AIC_earthworms[order(AIC_earthworms$AIC), ]

anova(earthworms_nb_add, earthworms_nb_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT
anova(earthworms_p_add, earthworms_p_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT
```

AIC is very similar between all models, though models without interaction have lowest AIC.
LRT shows no significant effect of adding the interaction.
The two additive models are provisionally retained.

```{r}
#| label: DHARMa model diagnostics for earthworm models

res_p_earthworms <- simulateResiduals(earthworms_p_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_p_earthworms)

testDispersion(res_p_earthworms)
testZeroInflation(res_p_earthworms)

res_nb_earthworms <- simulateResiduals(earthworms_nb_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_nb_earthworms)

testDispersion(res_nb_earthworms)
testZeroInflation(res_nb_earthworms)
```

Both Poisson and negative binomial models do not show any significant issues in DHARMa residuals, dispersion test and zero inflation test.
The Poisson model is retained because it has a slightly lower AIC and a more parsimonious structure (df lost 5, vs 6 in negative binomial).

```{r}
#| label: Model effects and pairwise comparison for earthworm model
Anova(earthworms_p_add)
summary(earthworms_p_add)

# Estimated marginal means for layers (response scale)
emm_layers_earthworms <- emmeans(earthworms_p_add, ~ layer, type = "response")
emm_layers_earthworms

# Pairwise comparisons (Tukey correction)
pairwise_layers_earthworms <- as.data.frame(
  pairs(emmeans(earthworms_p_add, ~ layer), adjust = "tukey")
)

# Back-transform estimates to abundance ratios
pairwise_layers_earthworms$ratio <- exp(pairwise_layers_earthworms$estimate)
pairwise_layers_earthworms

# Plot estimated abundance on the response scale
plot(emm_layers_earthworms)
```

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a significant effect of soil layer on earthworm abundance (χ² = 12.69, df = 2, p = 0.0018).
The effect of soil type was not significant (χ² = 0.35, df = 1, p = 0.557).
The estimated random-effect variance for monolith was 0.510 (SD = 0.714), indicating variation in baseline earthworm abundance among monoliths.
The model summary shows that estimates including layer were highly instable, with standard errors of around 10511.
Coefficients can therefore not be correctly interpreted for layers.

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment showed significantly higher abundance in layer 10 than in layer 20 (2.31 times).
No significant differences were detected between layer L and either layer 10 or layer 20 (both p = 1.000).
However, the estimated abundance of earthworms in layer L was zero with an unbounded confidence interval.
No earthworms were observed in layer L during the sampling, which explains the high errors in the models and the unbounded confidence interval.

## PERMANOVA

### Data preparation

```{r}
#| label: Data preparation for PERMANOVA and PCoA
df_perm <- df
# defining taxonomic abundance columns
community_cols <- names(df_perm)[7:ncol(df_perm)]

# remove zero-abundance samples (decision following vegan
#handbook, since zero-abundance layer does not convey community
#composition information)
keep <- rowSums(df_perm[, community_cols], na.rm = TRUE) > 0
df_perm <- df_perm[keep, , drop = FALSE]

# create the community matrix
comm <- as.matrix(df_perm[, community_cols])
storage.mode(comm) <- "numeric" # making sure its num

# define meta_layer for tested variables + monoliths
meta_layer <- df_perm[, c("monolith_ID", "soil_type", "layer")] 

# create Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix
dist_layer <- vegdist(comm, method = "bray")
```

### PERMANOVA layer effects

```{r}
#| label: Setting permutation scheme and fitting the layer PERMANOVA
# Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA
# define permutation scheme, limit WITHIN monoliths (due to
#spatial dependence of the three layers)
perm_layer <- how(
  nperm = 9999,
  blocks = meta_layer$monolith_ID
) # chose large number of perms for stabilizing p value, increase
#for borderline p values

# run based on defined scheme
permanova_layer <- adonis2(
  dist_layer ~ layer,
  data = meta_layer,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

print(permanova_layer)
# => significant, R2 16% 
```

PERMANOVA shows a significant effect of soil layer on macrofauna community composition (Bray–Curtis dissimilarity: F = 5.46, R² = 0.163, p = 0.0001).
Soil layer explained around 16.3% of variation in the community composition, indicating that macrofauna community composition differed significantly among layers.

```{r}
#| label: Betadisper homogeneity of variance test for layers
# check dispersion using betadisper (if significant, permanova
#result might only be due to unequal dispersion; a bit like
#homogeneity of variance in anova) / is like non-parametric
#Levene test

bd_layer <- betadisper(
  dist_layer,
  group = meta_layer$layer,
  type = "median",
  bias.adjust = TRUE
)

# same permutation scheme

dispersion_layer <- permutest(
  bd_layer,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

print(dispersion_layer)

# quick visualisation (PCoA)
plot(bd_layer)

```

Homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was assessed using a permutation test based on betadisper.
No significant differences in dispersion were detected for soil layers (F = 0.75, p = 0.321), suggesting that the PERMANOVA result was not driven by differences in within-group dispersion.

```{r}
#| label: Pairwise PERMANOVA for soil layers
# pairwise PERMANOVA testing for layers
layer_pairs <- list(
  c("L", "10"),
  c("L", "20"),
  c("10", "20")
)

# function based to apply to all pairs
pairwise_results <- lapply(layer_pairs, function(pair) {
  
  # Keep only the two layers being compared
  keep_pair <- meta_layer$layer %in% pair
  
  meta_pair <- droplevels(meta_layer[keep_pair, , drop = FALSE])
  
  # subset the original Bray-Curtis distance object for this pair
  dist_pair <- as.dist(as.matrix(dist_layer)[keep_pair, keep_pair])
  
  # restrict perms to monoliths, like in global PERMANOVA
  perm_pair <- how(
    nperm = 9999,
    blocks = meta_pair$monolith_ID
  )
  
  # perform PERMANOVA
  res <- adonis2(
    dist_pair ~ layer,
    data = meta_pair,
    permutations = perm_pair
  )
  
  #for nice table notation
  data.frame(
    comparison = paste(pair, collapse = " vs "),
    F = res$F[1],
    R2 = res$R2[1],
    p_value = res$`Pr(>F)`[1]
  )
})

pairwise_results <- do.call(rbind, pairwise_results)

# Correct for the three pairwise tests
pairwise_results$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(
  pairwise_results$p_value,
  method = "bonferroni" ) # Bonferroni correction

print(pairwise_results)
```

Pairwise PERMANOVA suggests significant differences in macrofauna community composition for all soil layers.
Significant differences were observed between L and 10 (F = 6.05, R² = 0.141, adjusted p = 0.0003), L and 20 (F = 4.55, R² = 0.110, adjusted p = 0.0003), and 10 and 20 (F = 5.76, R² = 0.132, adjusted p = 0.0012), using Bonferroni correction.

### PCoA for layers

```{r}
#| label: Represent layer composition in PCoA using Bray-Curtis distances
# calculate, using same distance matrix like in PERMANOVA
pcoa_layer <- cmdscale(
  dist_layer, k = 2, eig = TRUE, add = TRUE
) # set k for number of dimensions +> k = 2 two dimensional

# sample scores
pcoa_df_perm <- data.frame(
  PCoA1 = pcoa_layer$points[, 1],
  PCoA2 = pcoa_layer$points[, 2],
  layer = factor(df_perm$layer, levels = c("L", "10", "20"))
)

# calculate hulls around samples
hull_df_perm <- pcoa_df_perm %>%
  group_by(layer) %>%
  slice(chull(PCoA1, PCoA2))

# fit taxon abundances to the PCoA (using same permutation scheme
#as in PERMANOVA)
fit <- envfit(
  pcoa_layer$points,
  comm,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

# extract taxon results and adjust p-values (multiple testing)
taxa_results <- data.frame(
  taxon = rownames(fit$vectors$arrows),
  R2 = fit$vectors$r,
  p_value = fit$vectors$pvals
)

taxa_results$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(
  taxa_results$p_value,
  method = "BH"
) # BH adjustment for multiple testing (false discovery rate)

# extract taxon vectors 
vec <- as.data.frame(scores(fit, display = "vectors"))
vec$taxon <- rownames(vec)
names(vec)[1:2] <- c("PCoA1", "PCoA2")

# match adjusted p-values by taxon
vec$p_adjusted <- taxa_results$p_adjusted[
  match(vec$taxon, taxa_results$taxon)
]

# keep those with adjusted p < 0.05
vec <- vec[
  !is.na(vec$p_adjusted) &
    vec$p_adjusted < 0.05,
]

# calculate dim1 and dim2 percentages
eig <- pcoa_layer$eig
positive_eig <- eig[eig > 0]

pc1_pct <- 100 * eig[1] / sum(positive_eig)
pc2_pct <- 100 * eig[2] / sum(positive_eig)


# plot PCoA
p <- ggplot(pcoa_df_perm, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = layer)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = hull_df_perm,
    aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, fill = layer, group = layer),
    alpha = 0.12,
    color = NA,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = layer_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = layer_colors) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "PCoA of macrofauna communities by layer",
    color = "Layer",
    fill = "Layer",
    x = sprintf("PCoA1 (%.1f%%)", pc1_pct),
    y = sprintf("PCoA2 (%.1f%%)", pc2_pct)
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )


# taxon arrows and labels
  p <- p +
    geom_segment(
      data = vec,
      aes(
        x = 0, y = 0,
        xend = PCoA1, yend = PCoA2
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      color = "grey25",
      linewidth = 0.9,
      arrow = arrow(
        length = unit(0.2, "cm"),
        type = "closed"
      )
    ) +
    geom_label_repel(
      data = vec,
      aes(
        x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2,
        label = taxon
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      color = "grey15",
      fill = alpha("white", 0.6),
      label.size = NA,
      size = 3.5,
      fontface = "italic",
      box.padding = 0.6,
      point.padding = 0.5,
      force = 3,
      max.overlaps = Inf,
      min.segment.length = Inf,
      segment.color = NA,
      seed = 123
    )

print(p)
```

```{r}
#| label: Print taxa significantly associated with ordination
taxa_results %>%
  filter(p_adjusted < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(p_adjusted)

```

The first two PCoA axes accounted for 26.1% of the variation in macrofauna community composition (PCoA1: 15.8%; PCoA2: 10.3%).
The ordination showed partial separation of communities among soil layers.
Samples from layers L and 20 exhibited substantial overlap, whereas samples from layer 10 were more distinctly shifted towards the right of the ordination.

The envfit analysis identified four taxa significantly associated with the ordination: Isoptera (R² = 0.501, adjusted p = 0.0014), Chilopoda (R² = 0.183, adjusted p = 0.0014), Opiliones (R² = 0.155, adjusted p = 0.0103) and Lumbricina_oligochaetes (R² = 0.238, adjusted p = 0.0154).
Isoptera showed the strongest association with the ordination.

### PERMANOVA for soil types

```{r}
#| label: Create new community matrix for soil type accumulated per monolith
# sum across all layers within each monolith => to test
#independent of layer effects, since dependent of monolith
comm_mono <- rowsum(
  comm,
  group = df_perm$monolith_ID,
  reorder = FALSE
)

# one metadata row per monolith
meta_mono <- df_perm[
  !duplicated(df_perm$monolith_ID),
  c("monolith_ID", "soil_type")
]

# aligning matrix with metadata
comm_mono <- comm_mono[
  as.character(meta_mono$monolith_ID),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

Is aggregated per monolith since layers are not independent.
Only tests between soils on monolith level.

```{r}
#| label: Distance matrix, PERMANOVA and betadisper for soil type

dist_soil <- vegdist(comm_mono, method = "bray")
# Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA

permanova_soil <- adonis2(
  dist_soil ~ soil_type,
  data = meta_mono,
  permutations = 9999
) 

print(permanova_soil)
# not significant, no differences by soil type

# betadisper

bd_soil <- betadisper(
  dist_soil,
  group = meta_mono$soil_type,
  type = "median",
  bias.adjust = TRUE
)

dispersion_soil <- permutest(
  bd_soil,
  permutations = 9999
)

print(dispersion_soil)

# simple plot
plot(bd_soil)
```

PERMANOVA did not show a significant difference in macrofaunal community composition between soil types (F = 1.68, R² = 0.085, p = 0.139).
The test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was also non-significant (F = 0.11, p = 0.742), indicating no detectable difference in within-group dispersion between soil types.
